The marker union is every site found in at least one donor (math supplement, Section 5.1). Its size sets the cost of the
union counts, of gap filling and of every per-line table, so it is projected before a run over all donors. This notebook
(i) states what is known about the donors' populations and the union it implies, (ii) writes down the simulations that would
turn that into a predicted curve, (iii) fits empirical curves to the data we have, and (iv) reads the fits against the
demographic picture, including what to expect from other taxa. The simulations are not run: they are written here to be run
once the union over all samples exists. The math supplement's Section 5.6 summarises sections 3-4.

::: {.callout-note}
## In short

- **Demography (Chen et al. 2022).** Mexicana's effective size fell about threefold between ~30 and ~5 thousand years ago
  (MSMC2), and mexicana accessions carry about **6x** the private variation a neutral equilibrium predicts. Mexicana races are
  topographically isolated populations (Sánchez-González et al. 2018). Expected: real alleles saturate within a population,
  each new population adds a block of private alleles, and false alleles add a constant number per donor.
- **Simulations proposed** (section 2): the expected site frequency spectrum of the donors under (S1) mexicana's Ne history,
  (S2) races as demes, (S3) the Zea species tree with ZEAL's donor composition; Eq. 1 turns each into a union curve.
- **Empirical fits** (six mexicana donors, four races, the ones that pass the curve rule; two families off the curve shown
  apart): Michaelis-Menten ($U_\infty \approx 474$ thousand sites on chr10), Watterson, and Watterson with false alleles
  ($\varepsilon_f \approx 13$ thousand per donor): 245, 225 and 263 thousand sites at 10 donors. The false-allele term's
  linear growth is what sets the last apart (section 3.7). The five-donor fits overshot the sixth donor by 5-11 %
  (section 3.8).
- **A new race** (Zx.0160_P2, Chalco) adds a larger share of its sites than a race-mate but fewer sites, as its discovery
  finds fewer tier-A sites (section 3.2).
- **Reading.** Chen's numbers are genome-wide; scaled to our low-copy ranges (section 4), neither false calls (read-based
  precision 0.97, supplement Section 5.5) nor Chen's private SNPs account for most of the private term $\varepsilon_f$.
  It is about the size of the sites where read and assembly alignment disagree; what it holds is untested. The discovery
  sensitivity is not determined from Chen.
  Other taxa: Zea as a whole carries 2.3x mexicana's SNPs in Chen's panel, an upper bound for the union's growth when ZEAL's
  parviglumis and other donors are added.
:::

```{r setup}
library(data.table)

```

## 1. A demographic model of the donors

### 1.1 Who the donors are

ZEAL has 96 teosinte donors (`meta/samples.csv`). Mexicana races from the passport
table (`meta/accessions.csv`, J2Teo); teosinte races are "geographical populations spatially isolated by the topography in
Mexico and Central America" (Sánchez-González et al. 2018).

```{r donors-table}
knitr::kable(data.table(
  taxon = c("mexicana", "parviglumis", "diploperennis", "luxurians", "huehuetenangensis"),
  donors = c(43, 40, 6, 5, 2),
  `mexicana donors by race` = c("Mesa Central 21, Chalco 14, Durango 5, Nobogame 3", "", "", "", "")
))
```

### 1.2 What Chen et al. (2022) measured

Chen et al. resequenced 237 teosinte accessions (22x) with 507 maize lines. Their Supplementary Table 2 (diversity map),
Supplementary Table 4 (BPP demography), Fig. 2a (F~ST~) and Supplementary Fig. 3 (MSMC2 Ne through time) give:

```{r chen-diversity}
chen <- data.table(
  taxon = c("mexicana", "parviglumis", "diploperennis", "perennis", "luxurians", "nicaraguensis", "huehuetenangensis"),
  accessions = c(81, 70, 20, 19, 14, 14, 5),
  snps_M = c(31.32, 41.51, 11.66, 15.29, 9.04, 7.41, 7.99),
  taxon_specific_M = c(4.26, 5.97, 1.13, 1.70, 0.48, 0.37, 0.64),
  specific_downsampled_M = c(1.82, 1.14, 1.06, 1.70, 0.58, 0.41, 1.00),
  pi = c(0.00804, 0.00847, 0.00629, 0.01038, 0.00592, 0.00543, 0.00572),
  fst_mexicana = c(NA, 0.068, 0.277, 0.277, 0.290, 0.270, 0.248),
  fst_maize = c(0.158, 0.101, 0.356, 0.354, 0.364, 0.342, 0.330)
)
knitr::kable(chen, digits = 5, col.names = c(
  "taxon", "accessions", "SNPs (M)", "taxon-specific SNPs (M)",
  "taxon-specific, downsampled (M)", "π per bp", "F_ST with mexicana",
  "F_ST with maize"
))
```

F~ST~ with maize is Chen's cultivated panel (507 inbreds; B73's subspecies): parviglumis and mexicana are closest to maize
(0.101, 0.158), the other taxa 0.33-0.36, so B73 is the outgroup of Eq. 1 for every donor, nearer to some taxa than others.
All Zea together (744 genomes, maize included): 70.73 M SNPs, 16.90 M taxon-specific. Mexicana's chr10 windows (Fig. 2b data):
mean $\pi$ = 0.00903. SNPs specific to one accession (Fig. 2d data): mexicana median 402,200 per accession (166,559-518,710),
parviglumis 322,355.

**Ne through time** (Supplementary Fig. 3, MSMC2; values read off the figure, approximate):

| Time before present | mexicana | parviglumis |
|---|---|---|
| ~30 ky | ~82,000 | ~86,000 |
| ~20 ky | ~77,000 | ~86,000 |
| ~12 ky | ~60,000 | ~86,000 |
| ~8 ky | ~44,000 | ~76,000 |
| ~5 ky to now | ~27,000 | ~62,000, then ~49,000 since ~4 ky |

The perennial and Central American taxa (diploperennis, luxurians, nicaraguensis, huehuetenangensis, perennis) decline from
35-60 thousand around 50-100 ky to 10-25 thousand around 8-10 ky, then rise again (diploperennis and luxurians to ~42-47
thousand). BPP divergence times (Supplementary Table 4, years): the (maize, parviglumis, mexicana) clade 30,467; with
huehuetenangensis 67,800; with diploperennis and perennis 121,533; the Zea crown 124,233; Zea-Tripsacum 653,733. BPP's Ne for
mexicana is 171,508 (95 % HPD 146,817-197,008), on a different scale from MSMC2's; only the shape of the MSMC2 history is used.

### 1.3 The union under a coalescent

Take B73 as the outgroup: a union site is a position where at least one donor carries an allele different from B73. Under
infinite sites, such alleles arise (a) on the B73 lineage or on the donors' lineage before their common ancestor, carried by
every donor (the fixed differences, $C$ of them), or (b) on the donors' genealogy, carried by $k$ of the $n$ donors. Each donor
finds a carried allele with probability $\eta$ (discovery sensitivity), and calls $\varepsilon_f$ false alleles of its own. Then

$$
\mathbb{E}[U_n] = C\,\big[1 - (1 - \eta)^n\big] \;+\; \theta \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} \xi_k(n)\, \big[1 - (1 - \eta)^k\big] \;+\; \varepsilon_f\, n
\tag{1}
$$

with $\theta = 4 N_e \mu L$ over the sites considered and $\xi_k(n)$ the expected site frequency spectrum of $n$ donors in units of
$\theta$ (the expected length of the genealogy's branches that subtend exactly $k$ donors, scaled). **Demography and structure
enter only through $\xi_k(n)$.** For one population at constant size (Wright-Fisher equilibrium), $\xi_k(n) = 1/k$; with
$\eta = 1$ and $\varepsilon_f = 0$, Eq. 1 is Watterson's (1975)

$$
\mathbb{E}[U_n] = C + \theta \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} \frac{1}{k} = C + \theta H_{n-1}
\tag{2}
$$

How $\xi_k(n)$ departs from $1/k$:

- **A recent contraction** (mexicana, threefold over the last ~30 ky, recent relative to the current $2 N_e \approx 54$ ky):
  fewer singletons and low-frequency alleles than $1/k$, more at intermediate frequencies; the union saturates faster than
  $H_{n-1}$.
- **Structure** (isolated races, low migration): donors from one deme share recent ancestry; a donor from a new deme adds the
  long branches of that deme, a block of private alleles. The union grows by steps as demes are added.
- **Several taxa**: the same, at the scale of the species tree (Section 5).

### 1.4 The equilibrium baseline

zealgt-old notebook 01 (2026-09-26) used the large-population version of Eq. 2: site frequencies $p$ in the population with
the neutral spectrum $g(p) \propto 1/p$ (a flat spectrum as the contrast), a carried allele found with probability $\eta$,
no fixed differences and no false alleles:

$$
\mathbb{E}[U_n] = S \sum_{p} g(p) \left[ 1 - (1 - \eta p)^n \right], \qquad
\hat U_n = U_2^{\mathrm{obs}} \, \frac{\mathbb{E}[U_n]}{\mathbb{E}[U_2]}
\tag{3}
$$

```{r data}
# donors in the column order of patterns_8donors.tsv
donors <- data.table(
  donor = c(
    "Zx.0540_P3", "Zx.0570_P2", "Zx.0550_P4", "Zx.0580_P2", "Zx.0500_P2", "Zx.0090_P2", "Zx.0470_P2", "Zx.0160_P2"
  ),
  race = c("Durango", "Nobogame", "Durango", "Nobogame", "Mesa Central", "Chalco", "Mesa Central", "Chalco"),
  own_sites = c(32750, 48251, 85952, 82601, 9060, 7482, 16283, 19767),
  status = c(rep("on the curve", 5), rep("off the curve", 2), "on the curve")
)
good <- which(donors$status == "on the curve")
unions <- data.table(
  set = c("pilot pair", "first four", "attempt 1 six", "all eight"),
  donors = c(2, 4, 6, 8), sites = c(70210, 170729, 178300, 196645)
)
pat <- fread("union_rarefaction/patterns_8donors.tsv",
  header = FALSE, col.names = c("pattern", "n"),
  colClasses = c("character", "numeric")
)
z <- do.call(rbind, lapply(strsplit(pat$pattern, ""), as.integer))
```

```{r afs, fig.height = 5.5, fig.width = 11}
g <- (1:2000) / 2000
g1 <- head(g, -1)
spectra <- list(`neutral 1/p` = (1 / g1) / sum(1 / g1), flat = rep(1 / length(g1), length(g1)))
afs <- rbindlist(lapply(names(spectra), function(k) {
  rbindlist(lapply(c(0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.3), function(eta) {
    eu <- sapply(1:10, function(n) sum(spectra[[k]] * (1 - (1 - eta * g1)^n)))
    data.table(spectrum = k, eta = sprintf("η = %.2f", eta), donors = 2:10, sites = unions$sites[1] * eu[2:10] / eu[2])
  }))
}))
afs[, spectrum := factor(spectrum, levels = names(spectra))]
lab <- unions[, .(donors, sites, label = paste0(set, ": ", format(sites, big.mark = ",")), vj = c(1.6, -0.6, 1.6, 1.6))]
union_of <- function(s) unions[set == s, sites]
plot_curves <- function(curves, title, colour) {
  ggplot(curves, aes(donors, sites / 1e3, colour = eta)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
    geom_point(size = 1.5) +
    geom_point(data = lab, aes(donors, sites / 1e3), inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 4, shape = 21, fill = "black") +
    geom_text(
      data = lab, aes(donors, sites / 1e3, label = label, vjust = vj), inherit.aes = FALSE, hjust = -0.08,
      size = 3.5
    ) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
    labs(title = title, x = "Donors in the union", y = "Union sites (thousands)", colour = colour)
}
plot_curves(afs, "Equilibrium baseline (Eq. 3) and the observed unions", "Discovery sensitivity") +
  facet_wrap(~spectrum)
```

At 4 donors Eq. 3 gives
`r paste(round(afs[spectrum == "neutral 1/p" & donors == 4, range(sites)] / unions$sites[1], 2), collapse = "-")`x
(neutral) the 2-donor union; the first four donors gave `r round(union_of("first four") / union_of("pilot pair"), 2)`x. The
pipeline unions at 6 and 8 donors include the two donors off the curve (section 3.1). The equilibrium baseline
has no private term: neither the false alleles nor the demes of section 1.3.

## 2. Proposed simulations (not run)

Each simulation produces $\xi_k(n)$ for the donor sets of interest; Eq. 1 turns it into a union curve with $\theta$ from
Chen's $\pi$, $\eta$ and $\varepsilon_f$ from our data (section 4), and $C$ from the fixed differences (or fitted). Tool: msprime
with a demes model (demography as a YAML file), infinite sites, no recombination needed for expectations (or chr10's
recombination map to get the variance along the chromosome); about $10^4$ replicate genealogies per donor set.

| | Model | Parameters (source) | Donor sampling | Output |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **S0** | one population, constant $N_e$ | none | $n$ haplotypes | $\xi_k(n) = 1/k$: checks the pipeline against Eq. 2 |
| **S1** | mexicana, one population, piecewise $N_e(t)$ | Supplementary Fig. 3 steps (section 1.2; digitise the figure for exact values); generation time 1 year | $n = 1, \dots, 43$ | the contraction's effect on $\xi_k(n)$ and the union's saturation |
| **S2** | mexicana races as demes (Mesa Central, Chalco, Durango, Nobogame), each with S1's history, symmetric migration $m$ | $m$ swept so that within-race vs between-race diversity matches Chen's accession-specific SNPs (6x neutral, section 4) and mexicana's K = 2 | ZEAL's mexicana donors: 21 / 14 / 5 / 3 by race, added in random order and race by race | the step a new race adds; the 43-donor mexicana union |
| **S3** | the Zea species tree | BPP divergence times and Ne (Supplementary Table 4), MSMC2 histories per taxon, introgression ignored at first | ZEAL's 96 donors (43 / 40 / 6 / 5 / 2 by taxon), in random order and taxon by taxon | the union over all donors, and the block each taxon adds |

Calibration targets for S1-S3 (Chen's panel, 22x individual genomes): per-taxon SNP counts, taxon-specific and
downsampled taxon-specific SNPs, $\pi$, F~ST~ (section 1.2). Chen's samples are not ZEAL's donors (none of the six donors'
collection numbers is among them), so the simulations use Chen for the populations and ZEAL only for the sampling. The
targets should be Chen's counts **within our low-copy ranges** (their SNP positions intersected with `lowcopy_chr1-10.bed`),
not the genome-wide totals of section 1.2: the share of their SNPs in our ranges is unknown (section 4).

## 3. Empirical curves fitted to the data

### 3.1 The data

Eight mexicana donors from four races, chr10, tier-A sites (step 4 of variant discovery): the four Durango and Nobogame donors
of the first test, two Mesa Central and two Chalco donors (union test, `docs/runs/genotype_union_6donors_races_chr10.md`,
attempts 1 and 3). Own sites from the tier-A VCFs; unions from `BIALLELIC_UNION` (GENOTYPE runs: 2 donors job 1111642, 4
donors job 1134902, 6 donors attempt 1, 8 donors job 1152382). The **sharing pattern** of a union site is which donors' own
sites include it, $z \in \{0, 1\}^8$ (job 1152598, `union_rarefaction/patterns_8donors.tsv`; 255 patterns summing to the
eight-donor union). The Durango donors were collected about 2 km apart (Nombre de Dios, Durango), the Nobogame donors about
3 km apart (Guadalupe y Calvo, Chihuahua).

A donor enters the curve if its family's lines show what the donor carries (`docs/decisions.md`, 2026-10-11). Checked on
the lines' RTIGER calls at the union sites gap filling called ALT for the donor:

1. at most 4 donor segments per line;
2. segment dosage in the bands of good families: reads in REF segments <= 3 % ALT, in HET segments 30-55 %, in ALT
   segments >= 75 %;
3. the donor segments of the lines passing 1-2 cover >= 90 % of chr10.

Six donors pass. **Zx.0090_P2** covers 24 % of chr10, below the 5th percentile (46 %) of what its pedigree predicts
(1000 families simulated on its `meta/registry.csv` tree; the tail probability not computed): unusually low, worth a check
of the family against the registry. The simulation counts a position covered when any of a line's six plants carries a
donor allele, which RTIGER may call REF at 1/12 dosage, so observed coverage runs low against it for every family; the
six families on the curve still reach 93-100 %. **Zx.0470_P2** covers 73 %, within what its
small pedigree predicts (4 BC1 and 7 BC2 plants; median 90 %): its lines carry too little of the donor to confirm it. Both
also lose two thirds of their sites to the witness veto. The curve and the fits below use the **six donors on the curve**;
the other two are shown separately (section 3.2).

```{r data-tables}
knitr::kable(donors, format.args = list(big.mark = ","), col.names = c("donor", "race", "own tier-A sites", "status"))
knitr::kable(unions, format.args = list(big.mark = ","), col.names = c("union (pipeline)", "donors", "union sites"))
pat6 <- data.table(pattern = apply(z[, good], 1, paste, collapse = ""), n = pat$n)[pattern != "000000", .(n = sum(n)),
  by = pattern
]
knitr::kable(pat6[order(-n)],
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c(paste("pattern z,", paste(donors$donor[good], collapse = " ")), "union sites")
)
```

### 3.2 The rarefaction curve

As in species-richness rarefaction, donors are the samples and sites the species. The rarefaction curve is the mean union over
every set of $n$ of the $N$ donors, computed exactly from the sharing patterns:

$$
\bar U_n = \binom{N}{n}^{-1} \sum_{|D| = n} \; \sum_{z} N_z \, \mathbb{1}\Big[\max_{d \in D} z_d = 1\Big], \qquad n = 1, \dots, N
\tag{4}
$$

```{r rarefaction}
rarefy <- function(members) {
  subsets <- unlist(lapply(seq_along(members), function(n) combn(members, n, simplify = FALSE)), recursive = FALSE)
  rbindlist(lapply(subsets, function(d) {
    data.table(
      donors = length(d), set = paste(donors$donor[d], collapse = " + "),
      sites = sum(pat$n[apply(z[, d, drop = FALSE], 1, max) == 1])
    )
  }))
}
sub_dt <- rarefy(good)
rare <- sub_dt[, .(sites = mean(sites)), by = donors]
sets <- list(`curve six` = good, `curve six + Zx.0470_P2` = c(good, 7), `all eight` = seq_len(8))
rare_sets <- rbindlist(lapply(sets, function(m) rarefy(m)[, .(sites = mean(sites)), by = donors]), idcol = "donor set")
knitr::kable(dcast(rare_sets, donors ~ `donor set`, value.var = "sites")[, c("donors", names(sets)), with = FALSE],
  digits = 0, format.args = list(big.mark = ",")
)
```

```{r rarefaction-plot}
ggplot(rare_sets, aes(donors, sites / 1e3, colour = `donor set`)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) +
  labs(
    title = "Rarefied union (Eq. 4) by donor set", x = "Donors in the union", y = "Union sites (thousands)",
    colour = NULL
  )
```

```{r off-curve}
union_set <- function(m) sum(pat$n[apply(z[, m, drop = FALSE], 1, max) == 1])
adds <- data.table(
  set = c("curve six", "+ Zx.0470_P2", "+ Zx.0090_P2", "+ Zx.0470_P2 and Zx.0090_P2"),
  sites = c(union_set(good), union_set(c(good, 7)), union_set(c(good, 6)), union_set(c(good, 6, 7)))
)
adds[, added := sites - union_set(good)]
adds[1, added := NA]
knitr::kable(adds, format.args = list(big.mark = ","), col.names = c("union", "sites", "added to the curve six"))
```

Each donor off the curve adds `r format(min(adds$added[2:3]), big.mark = ",")`-`r format(max(adds$added[2:3]), big.mark = ",")`
sites, a few per cent of the union: they find few sites (7-16 thousand tier-A) and share most of them with the six. Zx.0470_P2
lowers the rarefied curve at every $n$ for the same reason.

**A new race against a race-mate.** Zx.0160_P2 (Chalco) has 10,925 union sites that none of the four Durango and Nobogame
donors has, 0.56 of its own; each Durango or Nobogame donor against the other three has 10-45 thousand such sites, 0.31-0.53 of
its own (run plan, attempt 3). The new race adds a larger share but fewer sites, because its discovery finds fewer tier-A sites
(19,767 against 33-86 thousand): discovery depth, not race, sets most of what a donor adds.

```{r curve-fits}
# harmonic number H_n, continuous in n: digamma(n + 1) + Euler's gamma
harm <- function(n) digamma(n + 1) - digamma(1)
models <- list(
  `Michaelis-Menten` = list(f = sites ~ um * donors / (k + donors), start = list(um = 3e5, k = 4)),
  `Watterson + false alleles` = list(
    f = sites ~ cc + th * harm(donors) + eps * donors,
    start = list(cc = 1e4, th = 5e4, eps = 1e4)
  ),
  Watterson = list(f = sites ~ cc + th * harm(donors), start = list(cc = 1e4, th = 5e4)),
  Logarithmic = list(f = sites ~ a + b * log(donors), start = list(a = 5e4, b = 5e4)),
  Power = list(f = sites ~ a * donors^b, start = list(a = 6e4, b = 0.7)),
  `Square root` = list(f = sites ~ a * sqrt(donors), start = list(a = 6e4)),
  `Negative exponential` = list(f = sites ~ um * (1 - exp(-k * donors)), start = list(um = 3e5, k = 0.2))
)
sym <- c(cc = "c", th = "θ_η", eps = "ε_f", um = "U_∞", k = "K", a = "a", b = "b")
emp <- lapply(models, function(m) nls(m$f, data = rare, start = m$start, control = nls.control(maxiter = 500)))
emp_table <- rbindlist(lapply(names(emp), function(k) {
  cf <- coef(emp[[k]])
  data.table(
    model = k, parameters = paste(sprintf("%s = %s", sym[names(cf)], signif(cf, 3)), collapse = ", "),
    rmse = sqrt(mean(residuals(emp[[k]])^2)),
    at_10 = predict(emp[[k]], data.table(donors = 10))
  )
}))
plot_fits <- function(keep, title) {
  cv <- rbindlist(lapply(keep, function(k) {
    data.table(model = k, donors = seq(1, 10, 0.1), sites = predict(emp[[k]], data.table(donors = seq(1, 10, 0.1))))
  }))
  ggplot(cv, aes(donors, sites / 1e3, colour = model)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
    geom_point(data = sub_dt, aes(donors, sites / 1e3), inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = "grey50", size = 2) +
    geom_point(data = rare, aes(donors, sites / 1e3), inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 4, shape = 21, fill = "black") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
    labs(
      title = title, subtitle = sprintf("black: rarefied union (Eq. 4); grey: each of the %d donor sets", nrow(sub_dt)),
      x = "Donors in the union", y = "Union sites (thousands)", colour = NULL
    )
}
mm <- coef(emp$`Michaelis-Menten`)
wf <- coef(emp$`Watterson + false alleles`)
# range of the predictions at 10 donors over a group of models, in thousands
at10 <- function(keep) paste(round(range(emp_table[model %in% keep, at_10]) / 1e3), collapse = "-")
fading <- c("Logarithmic", "Negative exponential", "Watterson", "Michaelis-Menten")
lasting <- c("Watterson + false alleles", "Power")
```

### 3.3 Michaelis-Menten

Species accumulation curves are routinely fitted with (supplement Eq. 21; Soberón and Llorente 1993)

$$
\bar U_n = \frac{U_\infty\, n}{K + n}
\tag{5}
$$

the asymptote $U_\infty$ and the number of donors $K$ that reach half of it. Fitted: $U_\infty$ =
`r format(signif(mm[["um"]], 3), big.mark = ",")`, $K$ = `r round(mm[["k"]], 1)`, RMSE
`r round(emp_table[model == "Michaelis-Menten", rmse])` sites. If each site is found by each donor with rate $k_s$ and $k_s$ is
gamma-distributed across sites (shape $\alpha$, scale $1/K$) (supplement Eq. 22),

$$
\bar U_n = U_\infty \left[ 1 - \left( 1 + \frac{n}{K} \right)^{-\alpha} \right]
\tag{6}
$$

which is Eq. 5 at $\alpha = 1$, the negative exponential as $\alpha \to \infty$, logarithmic growth (Fisher's log-series) as
$\alpha \to 0$ and power growth for $\alpha < 0$. Since $k_s \approx \eta p_s$, $\alpha$ is the shape of the spectrum near
$p = 0$: the neutral $1/p$ is $\alpha \to 0$; Michaelis-Menten is a spectrum with fewer rare alleles than neutral and a finite
pool of sites.

### 3.4 Watterson

Eq. 1 at equilibrium, $\xi_k(n) = 1/k$, with $\eta$ absorbed into the fitted constants and no private term: the union grows with
the harmonic number, like $\ln n$, and has no ceiling.

$$
\bar U_n = c + \theta_\eta H_n
\tag{7}
$$

```{r watterson}
wa <- coef(emp$Watterson)
wa_res <- round(residuals(emp$Watterson))
```

Fitted: $c$ = `r format(round(wa[["cc"]]), big.mark = ",")`, $\theta_\eta$ = `r format(round(wa[["th"]]), big.mark = ",")`, RMSE
`r format(round(emp_table[model == "Watterson", rmse]), big.mark = ",")` sites. $c$ is negative, which Eq. 2 does not allow
(fixed differences cannot be fewer than none), and the residuals follow a pattern, not noise (`r paste(format(wa_res, big.mark = ","), collapse = ", ")`
for $n = 1, \dots, 6$: above, below, below, below, above, above): the curve bends too early.

### 3.5 Watterson with false alleles

Eq. 7 plus the private term of Eq. 1 (supplement Eq. 23):

$$
\bar U_n = c + \theta_\eta H_n + \varepsilon_f\, n
\tag{8}
$$

```{r watterson-false}
wf_cor <- cov2cor(vcov(emp$`Watterson + false alleles`))
wf_se <- summary(emp$`Watterson + false alleles`)$coefficients[, 2]
```

Fitted: $c$ = `r format(round(wf[["cc"]]), big.mark = ",")`, $\theta_\eta$ = `r format(round(wf[["th"]]), big.mark = ",")`,
$\varepsilon_f$ = `r format(round(wf[["eps"]]), big.mark = ",")` per donor, RMSE
`r format(round(emp_table[model == "Watterson + false alleles", rmse]), big.mark = ",")` sites. $c$ is still negative; three
parameters on six points leave three degrees of freedom, so this is a consistency check.

### 3.6 The three curves together

```{r main-plot}
main_models <- c("Michaelis-Menten", "Watterson", "Watterson + false alleles")
plot_fits(main_models, "Rarefaction curve and the three fitted curves")
```

```{r main-table}
knitr::kable(emp_table[model %in% main_models],
  digits = 0, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c("model", "fitted parameters", "RMSE (sites)", "predicted at 10 donors")
)
proj <- data.table(donors = c(5, 6, 10, 20, 43))
proj[, `:=`(
  mm = predict(emp$`Michaelis-Menten`, proj), watterson = predict(emp$Watterson, proj),
  wf = predict(emp$`Watterson + false alleles`, proj),
  wf_real = wf[["cc"]] + wf[["th"]] * harm(donors), wf_false = wf[["eps"]] * donors
)]
knitr::kable(proj,
  digits = 0, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c(
    "donors", "Michaelis-Menten", "Watterson", "Watterson + false alleles",
    "of which c + θ_η H_n", "of which ε_f n"
  )
)
```

### 3.7 Why Watterson with false alleles diverges from the other curves

The curves agree on the six points and part beyond them, into two groups: those whose growth fades (logarithmic, negative
exponential, Watterson, Michaelis-Menten: `r at10(fading)` thousand sites at 10 donors, Appendix A) and those with a term that
never fades (Watterson with false alleles and the power curve: `r at10(lasting)` thousand).

1. **The data grow faster than a logarithm and slower than a line.** The free power curve puts the exponent at `r round(coef(emp$Power)[["b"]], 2)`. Watterson
   (Eq. 7) can only grow like $\ln n$; its residuals run above, below, then above (section 3.4), so it bends too early and falls short beyond the
   data. That is also why it needs a negative $c$.
2. **The $\varepsilon_f n$ term takes the excess growth.** With it, $\theta_\eta$ drops from
   `r format(round(wa[["th"]]), big.mark = ",")` to `r format(round(wf[["th"]]), big.mark = ",")`, $\varepsilon_f$ takes
   `r format(round(wf[["eps"]]), big.mark = ",")` per donor, and the RMSE falls from
   `r format(round(emp_table[model == "Watterson", rmse]), big.mark = ",")` to
   `r format(round(emp_table[model == "Watterson + false alleles", rmse]), big.mark = ",")` sites. Beyond the data the linear
   term keeps adding $\varepsilon_f$ per donor while $\theta_\eta H_n$ flattens; from about 10 donors $\varepsilon_f n$ is the larger
   part (table above).
3. **The split between $\theta_\eta$ and $\varepsilon_f$ is poorly determined.** Their estimates are correlated at
   `r round(wf_cor["th", "eps"], 2)` (standard errors `r format(round(wf_se[["th"]]), big.mark = ",")` and
   `r format(round(wf_se[["eps"]]), big.mark = ",")`): many combinations fit the six points almost equally and differ widely at
   10 donors and beyond, so the projection is less certain than these standard errors suggest.

**Where Michaelis-Menten puts the false alleles.** Eq. 5 has no private term, so a constant $\varepsilon_f$ per donor is absorbed
by both parameters: the only way it can imitate growth that never fades is to saturate later and higher, raising $K$ and
$U_\infty$ (for $K \gg n$, Eq. 5 is nearly the line $(U_\infty / K)\, n$). Fitting Eq. 5 to the full rarefied curve and to its
real-allele part only (Eq. 8 without $\varepsilon_f n$) shows the size of the effect:

```{r mm-split}
mm_real <- nls(sites ~ um * donors / (k + donors),
  data = rare[, .(donors, sites = wf[["cc"]] + wf[["th"]] * harm(donors))],
  start = list(um = 3e5, k = 4)
)
mm_split <- rbindlist(
  lapply(
    list(`full curve (real + false)` = emp$`Michaelis-Menten`, `real-allele part only` = mm_real),
    function(m) data.table(um = coef(m)[["um"]], k = coef(m)[["k"]], slope = coef(m)[["um"]] / coef(m)[["k"]])
  ),
  idcol = "fitted to"
)
knitr::kable(mm_split,
  digits = c(0, 0, 1, 0), format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c("Eq. 5 fitted to", "U_∞", "K", "initial gain U_∞ / K")
)
```

The private term more than doubles the asymptote and delays saturation. So $U_\infty$ is not a ceiling on real alleles, and once
donors keep adding false or population-private sites at a constant rate Eq. 5 will fall short. The real-allele part comes from
Eq. 8's split of $\theta_\eta$ and $\varepsilon_f$, which is poorly determined (point 3), so its $U_\infty$ is an illustration, not
an estimate.

### 3.8 The five-donor fits against the sixth donor

The five donors of the 2026-10-08 version (all six but Zx.0500_P2), their fits extended to six donors, against the six
donors' rarefied union:

```{r four-vs-five}
rare5 <- rarefy(setdiff(good, 5))[, .(sites = mean(sites)), by = donors]
emp5 <- lapply(models[main_models], function(m) {
  nls(m$f, data = rare5, start = m$start, control = nls.control(maxiter = 500))
})
check <- rbindlist(lapply(names(emp5), function(k) {
  data.table(
    model = k, at_6 = predict(emp5[[k]], data.table(donors = 6)), at_10 = predict(emp5[[k]], data.table(donors = 10)),
    at_10_six = predict(emp[[k]], data.table(donors = 10))
  )
}))
check[, observed_6 := rare[donors == 6, sites]]
knitr::kable(check[, .(model, at_6, observed_6, at_10, at_10_six)],
  digits = 0, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c(
    "model", "five-donor fit at 6", "observed at 6 (curve six)", "five-donor fit at 10",
    "six-donor fit at 10"
  )
)
```

The rarefied means at 1-5 donors are lower with six donors than with five, because Zx.0500_P2 finds few tier-A sites
(9,060 against 20-86 thousand); the curves are compared at the same $n$, not the same donors.

## 4. Interpretation in the light of the demographic model

Our counts are all within the low-copy ranges (`lowcopy_chr1-10.bed`: 367 Mb, about 17 % of the 2.2 Gb B73 genome, roughly
its unmasked part; chr10 26.1 Mb). Chen's counts are genome-wide. The share of **Chen's SNPs** that falls in our ranges is not
known: about 17 % if SNPs were spread evenly per base, more if Chen's filters on maize-mapped reads kept mostly SNPs in unique
sequence, up to nearly all of them. Every Chen number below is given at both bounds; intersecting Chen's SNP positions with our
BED would settle it (their VCF is not in `agent/papers/chen2022/`).

```{r chen-numbers}
bounds <- c(`17 % (even per base)` = 0.17, `~100 % (unique sequence)` = 1)
chr10_share <- 26.1 / 367
a_hap <- sum(1 / (1:161))
own <- range(donors$own_sites[good])
til18_diffs <- 444982
theta_pi <- 0.00903 * 26.1e6
eta_lo <- own[1] / til18_diffs
eta_hi <- wf[["th"]] / theta_pi
singletons_neutral_acc <- 2 * (31316555 / a_hap) / 162
# largest share of eps_f that false calls (precision 0.97) and Chen's private SNPs (upper bounds) explain together
explained <- (0.03 * rare[donors == 1, sites] + 402200 / 2 * chr10_share * eta_hi) / wf[["eps"]]
per_donor <- rbindlist(lapply(names(bounds), function(b) {
  private_real <- 402200 / 2 * bounds[[b]] * chr10_share * c(eta_lo, eta_hi)
  data.table(
    share = b, theta_counts = 31316555 * bounds[[b]] * chr10_share / a_hap,
    real_private = paste(format(round(private_real, -1), big.mark = ","), collapse = "-"),
    real_share = paste(round(100 * private_real / wf[["eps"]]), collapse = "-")
  )
}))
```

1. **Discovery sensitivity $\eta$ is not determined from Chen.** Routes to how much variation a mexicana haplotype carries in
   chr10's ranges:
   - Chen's chr10 $\pi$ (0.00903) times 26.1 Mb: $\theta \approx$ `r format(signif(theta_pi, 3), big.mark = ",")`, so
     $\eta = \theta_\eta / \theta \approx$ `r round(eta_hi, 2)`; this assumes Chen's per-base $\pi$ holds for every base of our
     ranges.
   - Chen's 31.3 M mexicana SNPs in our ranges, by Watterson ($H_{161} \approx$ `r round(a_hap, 2)`): $\theta \approx$
     `r paste(format(round(per_donor$theta_counts, -3), big.mark = ","), collapse = " to ")` at the two bounds, so
     $\eta \approx$ `r paste(round(wf[["th"]] / per_donor$theta_counts, 2), collapse = " to ")`; above 1 at the 17 % bound,
     which is impossible.
   - The TIL18 assembly differs from B73 at `r format(til18_diffs, big.mark = ",")` sites in chr10's ranges (AnchorWave), more
     than Chen's whole mexicana panel there at the 17 % bound: our donors' own sites give
     $\eta \approx$ `r sprintf("%.2f-%.2f", eta_lo, own[2] / til18_diffs)` (zealgt-old's ~0.1). This is the most direct route
     for our discovery; $\pi$'s `r round(eta_hi, 2)` is an upper value.
2. **The excess of private variation is genome-wide.** Under Eq. 2 the expected number of singletons equals $\theta$: Chen's
   31.3 M mexicana SNPs over 161 haplotype intervals predict about `r format(signif(singletons_neutral_acc, 2), big.mark = ",")`
   per diploid accession, and Chen observe 402,200 accession-specific SNPs, about
   `r round(402200 / singletons_neutral_acc)`x more. A contraction would give fewer; isolated populations, mapping errors and
   private insertions in repeats give more. Until Chen's SNPs are placed in our ranges, this excess is not evidence that
   population-private blocks dominate our union.
3. **What the private term $\varepsilon_f$ holds is not settled.** $\varepsilon_f$ counts the sites per donor that no other
   donor shares (`r format(round(wf[["eps"]]), big.mark = ",")`), not the donor's own sites (about
   `r round(rare[donors == 1, sites] / 1e3)` thousand, rarefied $n = 1$). Two sources can be sized:

   - **False calls** (reads do not show the allele): tier-A precision against the founder's own minibwa-aligned reads is
     $\approx 0.97$ on the simulated QC set (math supplement, Section 5.5), so about
     `r format(round(0.03 * rare[donors == 1, sites], -1), big.mark = ",")` false sites per donor, at most
     `r round(100 * 0.03 * rare[donors == 1, sites] / wf[["eps"]])` % of $\varepsilon_f$ even if every one is private.
   - **Real private SNPs as Chen counts them**: half of 402,200 accession-specific SNPs per haplotype, times the share in our
     ranges, times chr10's share (26.1 / 367), times $\eta$ = `r sprintf("%.2f-%.2f", eta_lo, eta_hi)`:

   ```{r eps-split}
knitr::kable(per_donor[, .(share, real_private, real_share)],
  col.names = c("Chen's SNPs in our ranges", "real private sites per donor", "share of ε_f (%)")
)
   ```

   Together they account for at most `r round(100 * explained)` % of $\varepsilon_f$. The QC set's precision against the founder assembly
   (0.68-0.74) is not a false-call rate: Section 5.5 finds the non-B73 base in the reads at normal depth at most of the sites
   it scores as false, where the assembly alignment places that sequence elsewhere or not at all. It measures the
   disagreement between assembly alignment and read alignment, which is about the size of $\varepsilon_f$
   (`r paste(round(rare[donors == 1, sites] * c(0.26, 0.32) / 1e3), collapse = "-")` thousand of a donor's own sites at
   0.68-0.74). This fits private sites that the reads carry but that are not orthologous SNPs, such as donor-only sequence
   aligned to B73. That has not been tested. The split between $\theta_\eta$ and $\varepsilon_f$ is itself poorly
   determined (section 3.7, point 3).
4. **Which curve.** Within one population the contraction predicts saturation of real alleles: the Michaelis-Menten shape. What
   keeps the union growing in Eq. 8 is $\varepsilon_f n$. False calls are too few to make it. So the union keeps growing
   through sites each donor carries alone in its reads, whatever their origin, and not through calls the reads do not
   support. Removing more false calls will not stop that growth. The gap between the two groups of curves (section 3.7) turns on
   whether a new donor keeps adding such sites at the same rate. The union test measured the step a new race adds in our
   ranges, which Chen's genome-wide numbers cannot give: the one good Chalco donor adds 10,925 sites the four Durango and
   Nobogame donors lack, fewer than a deep race-mate (section 3.2).

## 5. What to expect from the other taxa

ZEAL's donors are 43 mexicana, 40 parviglumis and 13 from three other taxa. In Chen's panel:

- **Parviglumis is close to mexicana** (F~ST~ 0.068, the lowest between teosinte taxa) but more diverse (41.5 M SNPs against
  31.3 M; $\pi$ 0.0085 against 0.0080) and with a smaller, later decline (MSMC2: 86 to 49 thousand). It shares much of mexicana's
  variation, but its 5.97 M taxon-specific SNPs (14 % of its SNPs) are a block the mexicana union does not contain, and its larger
  recent Ne means more low-frequency variation per donor.
- **ZEAL's three other taxa** (diploperennis 6 donors, luxurians 5, huehuetenangensis 2) are distant (F~ST~ with mexicana
  0.25-0.29) and carry 1.13, 0.48 and 0.64 M taxon-specific SNPs; with 2-6 donors each, they add their blocks almost entirely
  with their first donors.
- **An upper bound.** All Zea together carry 70.7 M SNPs against mexicana's 31.3 M (2.3x; maize included). The union of all ZEAL
  donors cannot grow by more than that factor over the mexicana union at the same depth of sampling, and will grow by less,
  since ZEAL has few donors of the distant taxa and Chen's maize-specific SNPs (1.5 M and 0.9 M, tropical and temperate) do not
  enter.

These ratios are genome-wide; they carry over to our ranges only if every taxon has the same share of its SNPs there, and
taxon-specific SNPs may sit more often in repeats, so they likely overstate what other taxa add in our ranges.
A first-order projection: the mexicana union at 43 donors times a taxon factor between ~1.2 (parviglumis-specific SNPs only)
and 2.3 (all Zea). Simulation S3 replaces that range with a curve; the union over all samples measures it.

## 6. Mexicana, 42 donors on chr10 (run 1273053, 2026-10-14)

```{r mx-data}
mx_donors <- fread("union_rarefaction/mexicana42_donors.tsv")
mx_carriers <- fread("union_rarefaction/mexicana42_carriers.tsv")
rare_exact <- function(cr) {
  n <- max(cr$carriers)
  data.table(donors = seq_len(n), sites = sapply(seq_len(n), function(k) {
    sum(cr$sites * (1 - exp(lchoose(n - cr$carriers, k) - lchoose(n, k))))
  }))
}
mx_pass <- rare_exact(mx_carriers[set == "pass"])
mx_all <- rare_exact(mx_carriers[set == "all"])
n_pass <- nrow(mx_pass)
u_all <- mx_carriers[set == "all", sum(sites)]
fit_all <- function(dt) {
  lapply(models, function(m) {
    tryCatch(nls(m$f, data = dt, start = m$start, control = nls.control(maxiter = 500)), error = function(e) NULL)
  })
}
mx_fit <- fit_all(mx_pass)
mx_fit8 <- fit_all(mx_pass[donors <= 8])
pred <- function(f, k) if (is.null(f)) NA_real_ else predict(f, data.table(donors = k))
mx_table <- rbindlist(lapply(names(models), function(k) {
  cf <- if (is.null(mx_fit[[k]])) NULL else coef(mx_fit[[k]])
  data.table(
    model = k, parameters = paste(sprintf("%s = %s", sym[names(cf)], signif(cf, 3)), collapse = ", "),
    rmse = if (is.null(mx_fit[[k]])) NA_real_ else sqrt(mean(residuals(mx_fit[[k]])^2)),
    aic = if (is.null(mx_fit[[k]])) NA_real_ else AIC(mx_fit[[k]]),
    d_aic = NA_real_,
    at_42 = pred(mx_fit[[k]], 42),
    k8_at_24 = 100 * (pred(mx_fit8[[k]], n_pass) / mx_pass[donors == n_pass, sites] - 1),
    k8_at_42 = 100 * (pred(mx_fit8[[k]], 42) / u_all - 1)
  )
}))[order(rmse)][, d_aic := aic - min(aic, na.rm = TRUE)]
```

The 42 mexicana donors of run 1273053. Each sequenced line is a plant pool: one punch from each of six plants of the
same NIL. A family has **balanced plant pools** when its lines pass the dosage check of `docs/decisions.md`
(2026-10-11; per-donor medians, criterion 3 not applied), and **unbalanced plant pools** when its HET segments read low
ALT, presumed from unequal contributions of the six plants:
`r nrow(mx_donors[status == "pass"])` balanced, `r nrow(mx_donors[status == "fail"])` unbalanced, Zx.0520_P4 has no tier-A
sites. Too many donors to list every subset (section 3.2), so the curve is the exact mean over all sets of $k$ donors
from each site's number of carrying donors $d$: $E[U(k)] = \sum_{\text{sites}} 1 - \binom{n-d}{k} / \binom{n}{k}$, the
same mean as Eq. 4. Inputs: `union_rarefaction/mexicana42_carriers.tsv` and `mexicana42_donors.tsv`
(`agent/union_mex42/write_carriers.R`).


```{r mx-table}
knitr::kable(mx_table,
  digits = c(0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1), format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c(
    "model", "parameters (balanced)", "RMSE (sites)", "AIC", "ΔAIC", "at 42 donors", "fit on k <= 8: error at 24 (%)",
    "fit on k <= 8: error at 42 (%)"
  )
)
```

Fitted on all `r n_pass` points, Michaelis-Menten has the lowest RMSE. Fitted on $k \le 8$ (the range of the earlier
tests) and carried out, it misses the observed union at `r n_pass` donors by
`r round(mx_table[model == "Michaelis-Menten", k8_at_24], 1)` % and the union of all 42 donors
(`r format(u_all, big.mark = ",")` sites, unbalanced families included, so not the same donor set) by
`r round(mx_table[model == "Michaelis-Menten", k8_at_42], 1)` %. The curve points are not independent (each is a mean
over the same donors), so RMSE and AIC rank the models but their differences carry no significance.

Residuals of each fit on all `r n_pass` points. A model that describes the curve leaves residuals without a trend;
a curve that bends too early or too late leaves a wave.

```{r mx-residuals, fig.width = 11, fig.height = 6}
mx_res <- rbindlist(lapply(names(mx_fit), function(k) {
  if (is.null(mx_fit[[k]])) {
    return(NULL)
  }
  data.table(model = k, donors = mx_pass$donors, residual = residuals(mx_fit[[k]]))
}))
mx_res[, model := factor(model, levels = mx_table$model)]
ggplot(mx_res, aes(donors, residual / 1e3)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  facet_wrap(~model, ncol = 4) +
  labs(
    title = "Residuals of the seven fits, balanced families", subtitle = "ordered by RMSE; same y-axis in every panel",
    x = "Donors in the union", y = "Observed - fitted (thousand sites)"
  )
```

```{r mx-plot, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 5.5}
mx_cv <- rbindlist(lapply(c("Michaelis-Menten", "Negative exponential", "Watterson + false alleles", "Power", "Watterson"),
  function(k) data.table(model = k, donors = seq(1, 42, 0.5), sites = pred(mx_fit8[[k]], seq(1, 42, 0.5)))
))
ggplot(mx_cv, aes(donors, sites / 1e3, colour = model)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 8.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(data = mx_all, aes(donors, sites / 1e3), inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = "grey60", size = 1.8) +
  geom_point(data = mx_pass, aes(donors, sites / 1e3), inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 2.5) +
  annotate("point", x = 42, y = u_all / 1e3, shape = 23, size = 4, fill = "gold") +
  labs(
    title = "Mexicana chr10: fits on k <= 8 of the balanced-family curve, carried to 42 donors",
    subtitle = sprintf("black: %d families with balanced plant pools; grey: all %d families with sites; gold: all-42 union",
      n_pass, nrow(mx_all)),
    x = "Donors in the union", y = "Union sites (thousands)", colour = NULL
  )
```

With the unbalanced families in (grey) the curve starts lower: they are the shallower donors, so a random set of $k$
holds fewer sites, and they add their sites late.

## Caveats

- Six donors, four races, all mexicana: every curve in section 3 fits them; the choice between curves rests on section 4,
  not on the fit. Discovery depth differs ninefold between them (9,060-85,952 tier-A sites), and two of the eight donors
  are off the curve.
- Zx.0500_P2 passes the curve rule on its lines' calls at union sites, but its own tier-A sites read a median 4.5 % ALT inside
  its lines' REF segments, against 1-2 % for the other five (artifacts present in all lines), so some of its sites in the sharing patterns are likely false.
- The rarefaction mean averages over donors; a donor with few lines or low coverage finds fewer sites and adds fewer.
- Section 4's numbers mix Chen's discovery (individual genomes, 22x, strict filters) with ours (BC1 pools); $\eta$ and the
  $\varepsilon_f$ split are orders of magnitude.

## Appendix A: other accumulation curves, set aside

All fitted to the same six points (Eq. 4); the table and plot include the three curves of section 3.

| Model | $\bar U_n =$ | Spectrum it corresponds to | Why set aside |
|---|---|---|---|
| Logarithmic | $a + b \ln n$ | neutral, large $n$; Eq. 6 at $\alpha \to 0$ | the same as Watterson |
| Power | $a\, n^{b}$ | $p^{a' - 1}$, $-1 < a' < 0$, $b = -a'$; Eq. 6 at $\alpha < 0$ | $b$ = `r round(coef(emp$Power)[["b"]], 2)` needs $g(p) \propto p^{-1 - b}$, rapid population growth, which Chen's MSMC2 history contradicts |
| Square root | $a \sqrt{n}$ | power with $b = 1/2$ | fixes the 6-to-1 donor ratio at 2.45, against `r round(rare[donors == 6, sites] / rare[donors == 1, sites], 2)` observed |
| Negative exponential | $U_\infty (1 - e^{-kn})$ | every site at one frequency; Eq. 6 at $\alpha \to \infty$ | no spread of frequencies |

```{r appendix-a}
knitr::kable(emp_table,
  digits = 0, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c("model", "fitted parameters", "RMSE (sites)", "predicted at 10 donors")
)
plot_fits(names(emp), "Every accumulation curve fitted")
```

## Appendix B: pattern-level models, set aside

These fit the 15 sharing patterns of the four first-set donors (`union_rarefaction/patterns.tsv`, their own union of
170,729 sites) instead of the rarefied points, with a discovery sensitivity per donor.
They are set aside because they have no false-allele or population-private class: the many private patterns (`0010`, `0001`)
can only come from rare alleles and high $r_d$, so their parameters absorb errors and structure. They are the starting point
for fitting S1-S3's spectra to the patterns (a likelihood that allows AIC and likelihood-ratio tests, and per-donor
predictions), once a private class is added.

### Version 2: a sensitivity per donor

$$
g_2(p) = (1 - \phi)\, \frac{p^{a - 1}}{\sum_{q} q^{a - 1}} + \phi\, \mathbb{1}[p = 1], \qquad
P(z) = \sum_{p} g_2(p) \prod_{d = 1}^{4} (r_d\, p)^{z_d} (1 - r_d\, p)^{1 - z_d}
\tag{B1}
$$

$$
\log L = \sum_{z \neq 0000} N_z \log \frac{P(z)}{1 - P(0000)}, \qquad \hat S = U_{1234}^{\mathrm{obs}} / (1 - P(0000))
\tag{B2}
$$

### Version 3: a shared class

A fraction $\phi$ of sites that every donor carries and finds with the same probability $e$ (the fixed differences $C$ of
Eq. 1); the rest as B1 without the point mass ($g_3(p) \propto p^{a - 1}$):

$$
P(z) = (1 - \phi) \sum_{p} g_3(p) \prod_{d = 1}^{4} (r_d\, p)^{z_d} (1 - r_d\, p)^{1 - z_d}
\; + \; \phi \prod_{d = 1}^{4} e^{z_d} (1 - e)^{1 - z_d}
\tag{B3}
$$

```{r pattern-fits}
# the four first-set donors, from their own union (job 1143239)
pat <- fread("union_rarefaction/patterns.tsv",
  header = FALSE, col.names = c("pattern", "n"),
  colClasses = c("character", "numeric")
)
z <- do.call(rbind, lapply(strsplit(pat$pattern, ""), as.integer))
p_rare <- function(zz, r, w, grid) {
  apply(zz, 1, function(zr) {
    q <- rep(1, length(grid))
    for (d in seq_along(r)) q <- q * if (zr[d] == 1) grid * r[d] else 1 - grid * r[d]
    sum(w * q)
  })
}
spectrum <- function(a) g^(a - 1) / sum(g^(a - 1))
model <- list(
  v2 = list(
    start = c(rep(-1, 4), -3, log(0.5)),
    par = function(th) list(r = plogis(th[1:4]), phi = plogis(th[5]), a = exp(th[6]), e = NA),
    pz = function(zz, m) p_rare(zz, m$r, c((1 - m$phi) * spectrum(m$a), m$phi), c(g, 1)),
    miss = function(rs, m) {
      sum(c((1 - m$phi) * spectrum(m$a), m$phi) * Reduce(`*`, lapply(rs, function(x) 1 - c(g, 1) * x)))
    }
  ),
  v3 = list(
    start = c(rep(-1, 4), -3, log(0.5), 1),
    par = function(th) list(r = plogis(th[1:4]), phi = plogis(th[5]), a = exp(th[6]), e = plogis(th[7])),
    pz = function(zz, m) {
      (1 - m$phi) * p_rare(zz, m$r, spectrum(m$a), g) +
        m$phi * apply(zz, 1, function(zr) prod(ifelse(zr == 1, m$e, 1 - m$e)))
    },
    miss = function(rs, m) {
      (1 - m$phi) * sum(spectrum(m$a) * Reduce(`*`, lapply(rs, function(x) 1 - g * x))) +
        m$phi * (1 - m$e)^length(rs)
    }
  )
)
fits <- lapply(model, function(md) {
  nll <- function(th) {
    pz <- md$pz(z, md$par(th))
    -sum(pat$n * log(pz / sum(pz)))
  }
  ft <- optim(md$start, nll, method = "BFGS", control = list(maxit = 2000))
  m <- md$par(ft$par)
  m$S <- sum(pat$n) / (1 - md$miss(m$r, m))
  m$union <- function(rs) m$S * (1 - md$miss(rs, m))
  m$fitted <- sum(pat$n) * md$pz(z, m) / sum(md$pz(z, m))
  m$loglik <- -ft$value
  m
})
par_table <- rbindlist(lapply(names(fits), function(v) {
  m <- fits[[v]]
  data.table(
    version = sub("v", "", v), r_0540 = m$r[1], r_0570 = m$r[2], r_0550 = m$r[3], r_0580 = m$r[4],
    a = m$a, phi = m$phi, e = m$e, S = round(m$S), log_lik = round(m$loglik, 1)
  )
}))
knitr::kable(par_table, digits = 3, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
knitr::kable(
  data.table(
    pattern = pat$pattern, observed = pat$n, version_2 = round(fits$v2$fitted),
    version_3 = round(fits$v3$fitted)
  )[order(-observed)],
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","), col.names = c("pattern z", "observed", "Version 2 (B1)", "Version 3 (B3)")
)
```

Version 2 goes to the edge of B1 ($\phi \approx 0$, $a \approx 0$) and predicts about half of the sites found by all four
donors (`1111`). Version 3 fits the patterns and the observed unions within 1 %, with a log-likelihood gain of
`r round(fits$v3$loglik - fits$v2$loglik, 1)` for one more parameter.
